title: API Request Blocker (rate limit + block)
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Sep 2026 ("API Blocking")
summary: Limit each client to `limit` requests per `window` seconds. A client that goes over is blocked for `blockFor` seconds.
statement:
Build a request filter for an API. It is created with three numbers: `limit`, `window` and `blockFor` (all in seconds).

`allow(clientId, timestamp)` is called for every incoming request, with timestamps that never decrease. It returns true if the request is accepted and false if it is rejected:

- If the client is currently blocked, reject. A client blocked at time t stays blocked for every timestamp before `t + blockFor`. Rejected requests are not counted and don't extend the block.
- Otherwise, look at the client's accepted requests in the last `window` seconds, i.e. with timestamps in `(timestamp - window, timestamp]`. If there are fewer than `limit`, accept and record this request.
- If there are already `limit`, this request is one too many: reject it, block the client starting now, and forget its request history.

Clients are independent of each other.

```
RequestBlocker(3, 10, 5)
allow("a", 1) -> true
allow("a", 2) -> true
allow("a", 3) -> true
allow("a", 4) -> false   // 4th within 10 s: blocked until 9
allow("a", 6) -> false   // still blocked
allow("a", 9) -> true    // block over, history was cleared
```
example: limit 3, window 10, blockFor 5: requests at 1, 2, 3 pass; 4 is blocked (until 9); 6 rejected; 9 passes.
hint: Per client: a queue of accepted timestamps (drop the ones that slid out of the window) and a blockedUntil time.

tests: 4th request inside 10 s is blocked; blocked until 9
blockFor 0: only the extra request is rejected
window is (t - 60, t]: the request at 0 has expired at 60
blocked requests don't extend the block or count

title: Job Scheduler (one-time and recurring jobs)
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite reports, Aug–Sep 2026 ("Job Scheduler")
summary: Schedule one-time and recurring jobs, cancel them, and advance a clock that returns the runs that are due, in time order.
statement:
Implement an in-memory job scheduler driven by a simulated clock (times are integers).

- `schedule(jobId, runAt)` — run `jobId` once at time `runAt`.
- `scheduleRecurring(jobId, firstRunAt, interval)` — run `jobId` at `firstRunAt`, `firstRunAt + interval`, `firstRunAt + 2·interval`, … (`interval ≥ 1`).
- `cancel(jobId)` — drop every run of `jobId` that `runUntil` hasn't returned yet. Return true if there was at least one such run, false otherwise (unknown id, already cancelled, or a one-time job that was already returned).
- `runUntil(now)` — move the clock to `now` (never decreases between calls) and return every run with time ≤ `now` that hasn't been returned yet, as strings `"jobId@time"`, sorted by time, then by jobId.

Scheduling a jobId that still has runs to come replaces its old schedule. A job may be scheduled at a time that has already passed; it is returned by the next `runUntil`.

```
schedule("backup", 5)
scheduleRecurring("report", 2, 3)
runUntil(4)  -> ["report@2"]
runUntil(8)  -> ["backup@5", "report@5", "report@8"]
cancel("report") -> true
runUntil(20) -> []
```
example: schedule(backup,5); recurring(report,2,3); runUntil(8) → [report@2, backup@5, report@5, report@8]
hint: A min-heap ordered by (time, jobId). Cancel lazily: keep a version number per job and skip stale heap entries.

tests: same time: ordered by job id; a finished one-time job can't be cancelled
runUntil only returns runs not returned before
scheduling an active id again replaces it
a job scheduled in the past runs at the next runUntil

title: CI Build Pipeline: minimum total time
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Aug 2026 ("CI/CD, Job Scheduling")
summary: Jobs with durations and "must finish before" dependencies run in parallel. Return when the whole pipeline finishes, or -1 if the dependencies have a cycle.
statement:
A CI pipeline has `n` jobs numbered `0 … n-1`. Job `i` takes `duration[i]` minutes. Each `deps[k] = [a, b]` means job `b` can only start after job `a` has finished.

Any number of jobs can run at the same time, and a job starts as soon as all of its dependencies are done. Return the time at which the last job finishes. If the dependencies contain a cycle, the pipeline can never finish: return `-1`.

```
n = 4, deps = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]], duration = [3,2,5,1]
job 0: 0–3, job 1: 3–5, job 2: 3–8, job 3: 8–9   ->  9
```
example: Diamond 0→{1,2}→3 with durations 3,2,5,1 finishes at 9 (critical path 0→2→3).
hint: Kahn's topological sort. A job's start time is the max finish time of its dependencies; the answer is the max finish time. Fewer jobs processed than n means a cycle. Follow-ups to expect: print a valid order (topological sort), only k workers, retries and failures, which jobs are on the critical path, re-running only what changed.
signature: int minimumTime(int n, int[][] deps, int[] duration)

title: Robot in an Unexplored Grid
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Aug 2026 (Round 4: navigate an unexplored grid with a robot)
summary: You can't see the grid. Drive a robot (rotate, move forward, detect walls, jump back to explored cells) to find the shortest path from its start to the target.
statement:
A robot stands somewhere in a rectangular grid that you can't see. Each cell is either free or a wall, and at most one free cell is the target. You control the robot only through the `Robot` object you're given:

- `turnLeft()`, `turnRight()`: turn 90° in place. The robot starts facing **up**.
- `moveForward()`: move one cell in the direction the robot is facing and return `true`. If a wall or the edge of the grid is in the way, the robot stays where it is and the call returns `false`.
- `isTarget()`: return whether the robot is standing on the target.
- `reposition(row, col)`: jump to a cell the robot has already visited and return `true`. For a cell it hasn't visited, nothing happens and the call returns `false`. Cells are numbered from the start: the start is `(0, 0)`, the cell above it is `(-1, 0)` and the cell to its right is `(0, 1)`.

You don't know the size of the grid, where in it the robot starts, or whether there is a target. Return the length of the shortest path from the start to the target, counted in steps of one cell up, down, left or right, or `-1` if there is no target or it can't be reached. The answer depends only on the grid: how many calls your exploration makes doesn't change it.

```
hidden grid:   S . .      S = start (facing up), # = wall, T = target
               # # .
               T . .

shortest path: right, right, down, down, left, left  ->  6
```

In the tests, a hidden grid is written with `0` = free, `1` = wall, `2` = target, followed by the start cell `[row, col]`. That's only how a test builds the robot: your code gets just the `Robot`.
example: Wall across the middle row: the shortest path is right, right, down, down, left, left = 6 steps.
hint: Keep your own map keyed by relative (row, col). Explore by BFS: for each cell taken from the queue, reposition there and try all four directions (turn, moveForward, then reposition back). The first time you stand on the target, its BFS depth is the answer. Without reposition, explore with DFS + backtracking and run BFS on the map afterwards.

title: Supply Drop I: nearest supply location
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Aug 2026 (Round 2, AI-assisted coding: graph navigation, part 1)
summary: Locations connected by routes with distances; some locations have supplies. Return the distance from the landing location to the closest supply location.
statement:
A rescue team lands at location `landing` and needs supplies. The map has `n` locations numbered `0 … n-1`. Each `routes[i] = [a, b, km]` is a two-way route of length `km` (≥ 1) between locations `a` and `b`. There may be several routes between the same pair. `supplies` lists the locations that have supplies.

Return the shortest distance from `landing` to the nearest location in `supplies`, or `-1` if none can be reached. If `landing` itself has supplies, the answer is `0`.

```
n = 6
routes = [[0,1,4],[0,2,1],[2,1,2],[1,3,5],[2,4,8],[3,5,3],[4,5,1]]
landing = 0, supplies = [3, 4]

to 3:  0→2→1→3 = 1+2+5 = 8
to 4:  0→2→4   = 1+8   = 9
answer: 8
```
example: landing 0, supplies {3, 4}: the best route is 0→2→1→3 with length 8.
hint: Weighted, non-negative edges → Dijkstra from the landing site. Stop as soon as you pop a supply location. (Unweighted → plain BFS. Many landing sites → multi-source: push them all at distance 0.) In the interview this came wrapped in a long business story: start by pinning down the nodes, the edges, whether edges are weighted or directed, and what counts as a target.
signature: int nearestSupply(int n, int[][] routes, int landing, int[] supplies)

title: Supply Drop II: pick up supplies, then reach base
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Aug 2026 (Round 2, part 2: "a transformed graph with additional constraints". The exact part 2 wasn't reported; this is a likely version.)
summary: A rescue team must get from its landing site to its base and stop at a supply location on the way. Return the shortest total distance.
statement:
A rescue team lands at location `landing` and has to reach its base at location `base`. On the way it must stop at **at least one** location that has supplies.

The map has `n` locations numbered `0 … n-1`. Each `routes[i] = [a, b, km]` is a two-way route of length `km` (≥ 1) between locations `a` and `b`. There may be several routes between the same pair. `supplies` lists the locations that have supplies.

Return the length of the shortest trip that starts at `landing`, passes through at least one location in `supplies`, and ends at `base`. The trip may visit a location or use a route more than once. If `landing` or `base` has supplies, that counts as the stop. Return `-1` if no such trip exists.

```
n = 6
routes = [[0,1,4],[0,2,1],[2,1,2],[1,3,5],[2,4,8],[3,5,3],[4,5,1]]
landing = 0, base = 5, supplies = [3, 4]

stop at 4:  0→2→4 (9), then 4→5 (1)       total 10
stop at 3:  0→2→1→3 (8), then 3→5 (3)     total 11
answer: 10
```

With `supplies = [3]` the answer is `11`: the shortest way to the base, 0→2→4→5 (10), passes no supply location, so the team has to go through 3.

The map is the same format as in Supply Drop I.
example: landing 0, base 5, supplies {3, 4}: stopping at 4 costs 10, stopping at 3 costs 11, so the answer is 10.
hint: Either run Dijkstra twice (from landing and from base) and take min over supply s of dist1[s] + dist2[s], or run one Dijkstra on a doubled graph: state (node, hasSupplies), with a free edge (s, 0) → (s, 1) at supply locations. The state-graph version also handles the usual follow-ups: limited fuel, at most k stops, one-way or closed routes.
signature: int supplyRun(int n, int[][] routes, int landing, int base, int[] supplies)

title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree (LC 366)
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Sep 2026 (Round 2: LeetCode 366 variant)
summary: Repeatedly remove all current leaves of a binary tree; return the values removed in each round.
statement:
Given the root of a binary tree, repeat until the tree is empty: collect the values of all leaves (nodes with no children) from left to right, then remove those leaves. Return the list of rounds.

```
        1
       / \
      2   3          round 1: [4, 5, 3]
     / \             round 2: [2]
    4   5            round 3: [1]
```

Trees in the tests are written in level order: `[1,2,3,4,5]`.
hint: Don't simulate removals. A node is removed in round = its height (leaf = 0, otherwise 1 + max height of its children). One post-order DFS puts each node in out[height].

title: Find Leaves II: general graph (follow-up)
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Sep 2026 (Round 2 follow-up: "change the tree to a general graph")
summary: Repeatedly remove the nodes that have no children from a directed graph (shared children and cycles allowed); return the nodes removed in each round.
statement:
You're given a directed graph with `n` nodes numbered `0 … n-1`. Each `edges[i] = [u, v]` means `v` is a child of `u` (read it as "`u` depends on `v`"). A node can have several parents, and the graph may contain cycles.

Remove nodes in rounds. In each round, the **leaves** are the nodes still in the graph that have no children still in the graph. Remove all of them at once and record them in ascending order. Stop when a round has no leaves.

Return the list of rounds. A node on a cycle never becomes a leaf, and neither does a node with a path into a cycle, so those nodes appear in no round.

```
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]]

    0         round 1: [3]
   / \        round 2: [1, 2]
  1   2       round 3: [0]
   \ /
    3         answer: [[3], [1, 2], [0]]
```

With `n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,1],[3,0]]`, nodes 1 and 2 form a cycle and nodes 0 and 3 lead into it, so no node is ever a leaf: the answer is `[]`.
example: Diamond 0→{1,2}→3 peels as [[3],[1,2],[0]]. If 1 and 2 point at each other, nothing ever peels.
hint: This is Kahn's topological sort run on the reversed edges: start with out-degree-0 nodes, and when a node is removed decrement the out-degree of its parents. Process level by level. The tree solution (height by DFS) breaks with cycles and double-counts shared children without memoization. Tell the interviewer what cycles do here: that's the main change from the tree version.

title: Progressive LRU, step 2: LRU Cache with TTL
source: LinkedIn Staff onsite report, Sep 2026 (Round 3, AI coding: progressive LRU implementation)
summary: An LRU cache where every entry also expires `ttl` time units after it was written.
statement:
Implement an LRU (least recently used) cache in which every entry also expires. Time is passed in as `now` on every call and never decreases.

- `LRUCache(int capacity)`: the cache holds at most `capacity` entries (`capacity ≥ 1`).
- `put(key, value, ttl, now)`: store `value` under `key`, replacing any value already there. The entry expires at time `now + ttl`: from that moment on it no longer exists. `key` becomes the most recently used.
- If `put` adds a **new** key while the cache already holds `capacity` entries, it first removes every expired entry. If the cache is still full, it then removes the least recently used entry.
- `get(key, now)`: if `key` is in the cache and hasn't expired, return its value and make `key` the most recently used. Otherwise return `-1`.

All values are positive. The least recently used entry is the one whose last `put` or successful `get` is the oldest.

```
LRUCache(2)
put(1, 10, 5, 0)
get(1, 4)  -> 10
get(1, 5)  -> -1      // expired at 0 + 5 = 5

LRUCache(2)
put(1, 1, 100, 0)
put(2, 2, 1, 0)       // expires at 1
put(3, 3, 100, 5)     // full: 2 has expired, so 2 goes and 1 stays
get(1, 6)  -> 1       //   (plain LRU would have evicted 1)
get(3, 6)  -> 3
```

This is step 2 of the progressive LRU exercise. Step 1 is the plain LRU cache (LeetCode 146).
example: put(1, 10, ttl 5, at 0): get at 4 → 10, get at 5 → -1.
hint: Keep the HashMap + doubly linked list from step 1 and store expireAt in each node. get checks expiry lazily. put on a full cache sweeps expired entries first (or keep a min-heap / TreeMap by expireAt to avoid the O(n) sweep), then evicts from the LRU end.

tests: expired entries are evicted before the least recently used one
